index.title: MIA Toolkit — one USB for all your scans
index.meta_desc: A free, private desktop app that turns a stack of hospital imaging CDs into one organized archive your radiologist can open from a single USB drive.
index.og_title: MIA Toolkit — all your imaging scans on one USB for your doctor
index.hero_alt: A stack of imaging CDs becomes one organized folder with a checklist, then a single USB drive.
index.h1: All your imaging scans, on one USB drive for your doctor.
index.lead: A free desktop app that turns a stack of hospital CDs into a single, organized medical-imaging archive any radiologist can open — without the technical headaches.
index.why_p1: If you or a family member has collected imaging CDs over the years — MRIs, CTs, X-rays from different hospitals — you know the problem: each disc is on its own, the discs are slowly degrading, and any doctor trying to compare studies across time has to juggle twenty different viewers. Important history gets lost in a drawer.
index.why_p2: This tool brings it all together. It copies each CD onto your computer, makes a plain-language inventory of every study, and builds one standards-compliant DICOM archive on a USB drive. Hand that single drive to your radiologist and everything loads at once — into any PACS or viewer.
index.why_p3: It is built for patients and the families helping them, for longitudinal review and second opinions. Your data never leaves your computer: there is no account, no cloud, no tracking, and no internet connection required to use it. It is not a diagnostic tool and does not replace professional radiological review.
index.step1_t: Insert each CD — or import a USB folder or a downloaded ZIP.
index.step2_t: See a clear spreadsheet of every study found across all your discs.
index.step3_t: Build one archive and copy it, verified, to a USB drive for your doctor.
index.note: Signed installers arrive with the first full release. For now this links to the source preview on GitHub.

help.title: How to use MIA Toolkit — step-by-step guide
help.meta_desc: A step-by-step guide to MIA Toolkit: copy your hospital imaging CDs, review every study, and build one organized DICOM archive on a USB for your doctor.
help.howto_name: How to organize your medical imaging CDs onto one USB
help.intro: MIA Toolkit turns a drawer of hospital imaging CDs, USB sticks, and portal downloads into one organized, standards-compliant archive on a single USB drive your radiologist can open. This guide walks through every screen — and answers the common questions.
help.overview_p1: If you or a family member has collected imaging over the years — MRIs, CTs, X-rays from different hospitals — each disc is on its own and slowly degrading. MIA Toolkit copies them all to your computer, makes a plain-language inventory of every study, and builds one DICOM archive on a USB drive. Hand that single drive to your doctor and everything loads at once, in any PACS or viewer.
help.overview_p2: It is free and open source, works fully offline, and your data never leaves your computer — no account, no cloud, no tracking. It is not a diagnostic tool and does not replace professional radiological review.
help.shot_home_alt: The MIA Toolkit home screen, with Guided Setup and the individual tools.
help.walk_intro: The easiest path is Guided Setup, which walks you through five stages. Here is each screen you will see.
help.s_welcome_p: Open the app and choose Guided Setup. The welcome screen explains the stages ahead. If you have used the app before, it picks up where you left off — you can even skip straight to building the archive.
help.shot_welcome_alt: The Guided Setup welcome screen outlining the steps.
help.s_add_studies_p: Add your imaging three ways: insert a CD and the app copies and ejects it automatically, import a folder from a USB drive, or import a downloaded ZIP from a hospital patient portal. Repeat for every disc — the app keeps a running count.
help.shot_add_studies_alt: The Add your studies screen with options to rip a disc, import a folder, or import a ZIP.
help.s_review_p: The app scans everything you added and lists every study it found. Open the spreadsheet to see a clear, plain-language inventory — patient, study, date, and modality. If discs from more than one person are mixed in, it warns you.
help.shot_review_alt: The Review screen showing the study count and a button to open the inventory spreadsheet.
help.s_documents_p: Add report or lab PDFs so they travel with the images. The app also finds PDFs already on the discs you imported. Tick the ones to include, and they are saved as plain files your doctor can open and embedded into the archive.
help.shot_documents_alt: The Add documents screen listing report PDFs with checkboxes.
help.s_build_deliver_p: Build the archive — the app combines everything into one standards-compliant DICOMDIR. Then choose your USB drive and copy. Every file is verified by checksum as it copies, so a failing or fake drive is caught instead of silently corrupting your scans.
help.shot_build_deliver_alt: The Build and deliver screen with build and copy-to-USB buttons and per-study progress.
help.s_done_p: That is it. The screen shows where the archive landed on the USB; you can open the folder or the inventory, or add more files. Hand the single USB drive to your doctor — everything loads together.
help.shot_done_alt: The Done screen confirming the archive was delivered to the USB.
help.task_cd_h3: Open a hospital imaging CD on Mac or Windows
help.task_cd_p: Insert the disc in Add your studies and the app copies it for you — no separate CD viewer needed, even if the disc’s own software won’t run on your computer.
help.task_merge_h3: Combine many discs onto one USB
help.task_merge_p: Add every disc, then build one archive and copy it to a USB. Years of scans from different hospitals end up in a single organized drive.
help.task_import_h3: Import a USB folder or a portal ZIP
help.task_import_p: No disc? Import a folder from a USB drive, or a ZIP you downloaded from a hospital patient portal — the same review and build steps follow.
help.task_docs_p: Include written reports alongside the images so your doctor has the full picture in one place.
help.task_deliver_h3: Give the archive to your radiologist
help.task_deliver_p: Hand over the one USB drive. It opens in any PACS or DICOM viewer, so every prior study can be compared at once.
help.trouble_cd_h3: A CD won’t read or is scratched
help.trouble_cd_p: Clean the disc and try again; old discs read slowly, so give it time. If a disc is unreadable, the others still import — you can deliver what was recovered and note the gap.
help.trouble_slow_h3: The copy is extremely slow or looks frozen
help.trouble_slow_p: Small medical files are slow to copy, so the progress can crawl — that is normal. But a copy running at a tiny fraction of normal speed usually means a failing or counterfeit USB stick; try a different, good-quality drive.
help.trouble_multi_p: That means discs from more than one person were added. Check the inventory spreadsheet and remove anything that does not belong before building, so each person’s archive stays separate.
help.trouble_win_p: The Windows installer is not code-signed yet, so Windows may show a SmartScreen prompt. Choose More info, then Run anyway. The macOS build is signed and notarized; Windows signing is on the way.
help.trouble_nodicom_h3: A disc has no images the app can find
help.trouble_nodicom_p: Some discs only contain a viewer, not standard DICOM images. MIA Toolkit detects DICOM by its content, not the file extension — but if a disc truly holds no DICOM data, there is nothing to import from it.
help.faq_a1: Yes — free and open source for patients and families, forever. Donations and institutional licenses keep it that way, but individuals never pay.
help.faq_q2: Is my data private? Does it upload anything?
help.faq_a2: Everything stays on your computer. There is no account, no cloud, and no tracking, and the app does not need an internet connection to work.
help.faq_a3: DICOM is the standard format medical images are stored in; a DICOMDIR is the index file that lets a viewer or hospital PACS load a whole archive at once. MIA Toolkit builds both for you.
help.faq_a4: No. It organizes, copies, and delivers your images — it does not interpret them, is not a medical device, and does not replace professional radiological review.
help.faq_q5: Which computers does it run on?
help.faq_a5: macOS 12 or newer, and Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit).
help.faq_a6: No. The app works completely offline; you only need a connection to download it the first time.
help.faq_q7: Can my doctor open the USB?
help.faq_a7: Yes. The archive is standards-compliant DICOM, so it loads in any hospital PACS or DICOM viewer.
help.faq_q8: My images came as a ZIP from a portal — can I use those?
help.faq_a8: Yes. Import the ZIP in Add your studies and it is treated like any other source.
help.cta_p: Free, forever. Download it, organize your scans, and bring them to your next appointment on one USB.
support.title: Support — MIA Toolkit
support.meta_desc: Why we believe your medical records belong to you, and how fair support keeps this tool free for everyone.
support.og_title: Support MIA Toolkit — your medical history belongs to you
support.h1: Your medical history belongs to you.
support.big: Your scans are a record of your own body — yet they're trapped on fragile discs, in formats built for institutions, not people.
support.p1: When you can't easily gather and carry your own history, you get worse care: repeated scans, missed comparisons, second opinions that start from zero. We think that's wrong. The images are yours; you should be able to hold them in one place, on any computer, and hand them to any doctor.
support.p2: So this tool is free, and it always will be. No account, no cloud, no company watching — your data never leaves your machine. We sign and notarize the apps so they open without scary warnings, for everyone, as soon as we possibly can. We will not put a paywall between a person and their own records.
support.p3: But signing certificates, translations, and the time to keep this working do cost money. If you can, support the project so it stays free for the people who can't — an older parent in another country, a family paying out of pocket, a clinic with no budget. Pay what's fair where you live. If now isn't the time, just download it. That's the deal.
support.where_p: Every contribution keeps MIA Toolkit free and signed for the people who can't pay — an older parent abroad, a family paying out of pocket, a clinic with no budget. One-time or monthly, it all funds the same thing: free access for everyone.
support.org_p: You can sponsor free access for a community, fund a new language translation, or support a regional rollout. Institutional sponsorship is what keeps the tool free for individual patients everywhere.
privacy.title: Privacy Policy — MIA Toolkit
privacy.meta_desc: MIA Toolkit is built so we can't see your data: offline app, no account, no telemetry, no cookies, no tracking.
privacy.intro: MIA Toolkit is built so that we can't see your data — not "we promise not to look," but "there is nothing for us to look at." This page explains exactly what that means.
privacy.app_li1: Runs completely offline. The internet is only needed once, to download it.
privacy.app_li3: No telemetry, no analytics — the app sends nothing, ever, to anyone. One exception you control: clicking "Check for Updates" fetches a single version file from our website; it carries no personal data or identifiers.
privacy.app_li4: Your medical images never leave your computer (or the USB drive you copy them to). We operate no servers and never see, receive, or store them.
privacy.app_li5: The app saves only a small settings file on your own computer (for example, your language choice).
privacy.site_li1: A static site with no cookies, no analytics, no trackers, and no ads.
privacy.site_li2: It stores one value in your browser's local storage — your language preference — which never leaves your browser.
privacy.site_li3: Hosting is provided by GitHub Pages, and downloads by GitHub Releases; GitHub may process standard technical request data (such as IP addresses) as described in GitHub's privacy statement.
privacy.site_li4: Optional support payments are processed by Lemon Squeezy as merchant of record, under their own privacy policy. We never see your card details.
privacy.email_p: If you write to us, we use your email address only to reply. No mailing lists, no sharing.
privacy.never_p: We never sell data, build profiles, track you across sites, or collect your medical information — we couldn't even if we wanted to; it stays on your machine.
privacy.changes_p: If this policy changes, the new version will be posted here with an updated effective date.
footer.disclaimer: This software helps you organize and deliver your own medical images. It does not interpret images, is not a medical device, and does not replace professional radiological review. No warranty.
footer.ethos: Open source · Private by design · No tracking
inst.includes: Every license includes a license certificate, an invoice for procurement, priority email support, an IT deployment guide, and a security one-pager — and it funds free access for patients everywhere.
inst.note: Individuals never pay. The software is identical and MIT-licensed; the institutional license is the compliance and support package on top.
stats.title: Transparency — MIA Toolkit
stats.meta_desc: Our download and traffic numbers, published in the open — the way we publish our code.
stats.intro: We publish our numbers the way we publish our code: in the open. Everything below comes from the aggregate counters GitHub already keeps — no cookies, no tracking, no personal data.
stats.chart_pending: The daily chart appears once a few days of history accumulate.
stats.method: How this is measured: GitHub counts release downloads and repository traffic in aggregate; a daily job snapshots those public counters into this page. Nobody is tracked, and the app itself never sends anything.
privacy.site_li1_gc: A static site with no cookies, no trackers, and no ads. We use GoatCounter, an open-source, cookieless counter, for aggregate page-view counts — it stores no personal data, builds no profiles, and does no cross-site tracking.
